C0.quote: Like many social choice/voting mechanisms, spatial social choice is
C0.note: Spatial social choice: a selection rule aggregates agents' submitted ideal points into one collective outcome, and the strategic aspects are studied. The paper also mentions facility location, but treats the setting as a voting mechanism.

C1.quote: we use the price of anarchy to quantify the impact of manipulation
C1.note: Most main theorems bound the price of anarchy (WD) under equilibrium refinements (EQ). Some results concern strategy-proofness (SB).

C2.1.value: submitted preference profile; submitted ideal point; submitted preferences
C2.1.quote: The collection of all submitted ideal points is the submitted profile

C2.2.quote: agent 𝑣 submits a submitted ideal point 𝜋¯𝑣 ∈ X
C2.2.note: Inputs are points in a compact convex domain X ⊆ R^k.

C2.3.quote: Each agent 𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 has an ideal point 𝜋 𝑣 ∈ X
C2.3.note: The held attitudes are sincere ideal points and an l_p cost function.

C2.4.quote: In practice, agents will not necessarily submit honest preferences.
C2.4.note: The paper uses separate notation: π_v for sincere ideal points and π̄_v for submitted ones.

C3.1.quote: This manipulation of submitted preferences results in the following
C3.1.note: All main analyses concern the Strategic Spatial Social Choice Game. Strategy-proofness results also consider possible deviations.

C4.1.note: Input format is OTH (spatial points) only.

C5.1.quote: how much worse an outcome obtained from a Nash equilibrium is
C5.1.note: The price of anarchy of the social cost (total distance) is used in the main results.

C5.2.quote: with respect to the sincere preferences Π, the outcome actually costs
C5.2.note: Social cost C(Π, r(Π̄)) is evaluated on sincere ideal points.

VOT.quote_info: no agent 𝑣 would obtain an outcome they sincerely prefer
VOT.note: Pure Nash equilibrium analysis implies that agents know others' submissions. Only the mechanism is stated as common knowledge; the abstract calls preferences private information. Agents are refined as minimally dishonest.

DES.note: Mechanism design (domain restriction) is discussed, but the designer is not modelled as an acting agent.

C8.1.quote: A set of submitted preferences Π̄ forms a pure strategy Nash equilibrium
C8.1.note: The minimally dishonest Nash equilibrium is a refinement of NE, so it is covered by NE. DOM: strategy-proofness results such as Theorem 4.3 and Definition 3.3.

C8.2.quote: we introduce the Minimally Dishonest Nash equilibrium refinement

C9.2.quote: If a point's cost has an intrinsic correspondence to its quality
C9.2.note: Stated: the relation between inputs and held attitudes, strategic minimally dishonest behaviour, and the cost-quality link (conditionally). Unstated: the information assumption needed for agents to reach Nash play, i.e. that they know others' submissions; only the mechanism is stated as common knowledge.

C8.1.reason: The minimally dishonest refinement is still a Nash equilibrium concept, so NE covers it and a separate OTH code is not needed.

C9.2.reason: The claims about real manipulation and rule assessment rely on agents reaching Nash equilibria, which needs an information assumption that the paper never states.
